edges.description: NF1 loss removes RAS-GAP restraint, hyperactivating RAS-MAPK signalling.
NF2 loss eliminates merlin, de-repressing mitogenic and Hippo/YAP-TAZ signalling.
Germline SMARCB1/LZTR1 loss cooperates with somatic 22q loss and NF2 inactivation in schwannomatosis.
RAS-MAPK hyperactivation drives Schwann-cell neurofibroma initiation.
Merlin loss removes contact-dependent restraint, driving neoplastic Schwann-cell proliferation.
Convergent NF2/merlin loss drives multiple non-vestibular schwannomas.
NF1-arm Schwann-cell tumorigenesis produces cutaneous neurofibromas.
NF2-arm tumorigenesis produces bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
Schwannomatosis-arm tumorigenesis produces multiple non-vestibular schwannomas.

nodes.description: The anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody bevacizumab is a targeted therapy for rapidly growing NF2-related vestibular schwannomas, and has shown clinical benefit in some individuals with NF2-associated ependymoma.

evidence.snippet: The VEGF antibody bevacizumab for rapidly growing vestibular schwannomas; bevacizumab has also shown some clinical benefit in some individuals with ependymoma.

nodes.description: Bilateral schwannomas of the vestibular division of the eighth cranial nerve; the defining feature of NF2-related schwannomatosis, producing tinnitus, hearing loss and balance dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: NF2-related schwannomatosis (NF2) is characterized by bilateral vestibular schwannomas with associated symptoms of tinnitus, hearing loss, and balance dysfunction.

nodes.description: Chronic, often debilitating pain is the most prominent and most frequently presenting feature of schwannomatosis, distinguishing it clinically from NF2-related disease.

evidence.snippet: The most common presenting feature is localized or diffuse pain or asymptomatic mass.

nodes.description: Schwannomatosis schwannomas arise through a composite four-hit / three-event mechanism: the germline first hit in SMARCB1 or LZTR1, somatic loss of the remaining wild-type SMARCB1/LZTR1 allele, and somatic biallelic inactivation of NF2. Because SMARCB1, LZTR1 and NF2 all reside on chromosome 22q, a single somatic 22q loss can co-remove the predisposition-gene allele and one NF2 allele, leaving a second somatic NF2 mutation to eliminate merlin — so this arm converges on the same merlin-loss effector as NF2-related disease.

evidence.reference_title: Evidence of a four-hit mechanism involving SMARCB1 and NF2 in schwannomatosis-associated schwannomas.
evidence.snippet: a four-hit mechanism involving the SMARCB1 and NF2 genes may be implicated in schwannomatosis-related tumorigenesis

evidence.reference_title: Germline loss-of-function mutations in LZTR1 predispose to an inherited disorder of multiple schwannomas.
evidence.snippet: schwannomas involved somatic loss of one copy of 22q, encompassing SMARCB1 and NF2, with a different somatic mutation of the other NF2 allele in every schwannoma

nodes.description: Benign peripheral nerve-sheath tumors of Schwann-cell lineage; the characteristic and frequently diagnostic tumor of NF1.

evidence.snippet: characterized by multiple café au lait macules, intertriginous freckling, multiple cutaneous neurofibromas

nodes.description: Each neurofibromatosis entity begins with a germline heterozygous loss-of-function variant in a Schwann-cell-relevant tumor suppressor — NF1 (neurofibromin) in NF1, NF2 (merlin) in NF2-related schwannomatosis, and SMARCB1 or LZTR1 in schwannomatosis. This germline first hit predisposes the Schwann-cell lineage to a somatic second hit that completes biallelic inactivation in tumor tissue (two-hit tumor-suppressor mechanism).

biological_processes: negative regulation of cell population proliferation

evidence.snippet: NF1 is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

evidence.reference_title: Evidence of a four-hit mechanism involving SMARCB1 and NF2 in schwannomatosis-associated schwannomas.
evidence.snippet: A novel germline SMARCB1 mutation was found in one patient; inactivating somatic mutations of NF2, associated with loss of heterozygosity (LOH) of 22q, were found in two schwannomas of this patient.

meta.association: Germline loss-of-function variants in LZTR1 (a CUL3 ubiquitin-ligase substrate adaptor) cause LZTR1-related schwannomatosis.

evidence.reference_title: Germline loss-of-function mutations in LZTR1 predispose to an inherited disorder of multiple schwannomas.
evidence.snippet: Our findings identify LZTR1 as a gene predisposing to an autosomal dominant inherited disorder of multiple schwannomas in ∼80% of 22q-related schwannomatosis cases lacking mutation in SMARCB1.

nodes.description: Oral MEK1/2 inhibitor selumetinib suppresses the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signalling driven by neurofibromin loss and is approved for symptomatic, inoperable NF1-associated plexiform neurofibromas.

evidence.snippet: The phase 2 trial (SPRINT) of selumetinib in pNF resulted in at least 20% reduction in the size of pNF from baseline in 71% of patients and was associated with clinically meaningful improvements.

nodes.description: In NF2-related schwannomatosis, biallelic NF2 inactivation eliminates merlin/schwannomin. Merlin normally enforces contact-dependent growth inhibition by limiting delivery of growth-factor receptors to the Schwann-cell surface and by restraining Hippo/YAP-TAZ-TEAD transcriptional output; its loss de-represses mitogenic receptor signalling and YAP/TAZ-driven proliferation. The same merlin-loss lesion is the convergent driver of sporadic and schwannomatosis-associated schwannomas.

evidence.reference_title: Genetic Alterations in Patients with NF2-Related Schwannomatosis and Sporadic Vestibular Schwannomas.
evidence.snippet: Biallelic NF2 inactivation primarily drives vestibular schwannoma tumorigenesis.

evidence.reference_title: Merlin regulates transmembrane receptor accumulation and signaling at the plasma membrane in primary mouse Schwann cells and in human schwannomas.
evidence.snippet: merlin regulates contact inhibition of proliferation by limiting the delivery of several growth factor receptors at the plasma membrane of primary SCs.

evidence.reference_title: Inhibition of YAP/TAZ-driven TEAD activity prevents growth of NF2-null schwannoma and meningioma.
evidence.snippet: driven by the TAZ protein in human and mouse NF2-null schwannoma cells

nodes.description: Because chronic pain dominates schwannomatosis, a comprehensive multimodal approach to pain management guided by a pain specialist or neurologist is recommended.

evidence.snippet: Comprehensive, multimodal approach to pain management, guided by a pain management specialist or neurologist

nodes.description: Multiple benign non-intradermal schwannomas of peripheral, spinal and cranial nerves, characteristically sparing the vestibular nerves; the defining feature of SMARCB1/LZTR1-related schwannomatosis.

evidence.snippet: LZTR1- and SMARCB1-related schwannomatosis are characterized by a predisposition to develop multiple non-intradermal schwannomas.

meta.association: Germline heterozygous loss-of-function variants in NF1 (neurofibromin, a RAS-GAP) cause neurofibromatosis type 1.

evidence.reference_title: A RASopathy gene commonly mutated in cancer: the neurofibromatosis type 1 tumour suppressor.
evidence.snippet: The NF1 gene encodes a RAS GTPase-activating protein called neurofibromin and is one of several genes that (when mutant) affect RAS-MAPK signalling, causing related diseases collectively known as RASopathies.

meta.association: Germline loss-of-function variants in NF2 (merlin/schwannomin) cause NF2-related schwannomatosis.

evidence.reference_title: Pathogenic Variants and Allele Loss of the NF2 and LZTR1 Gene in Sporadic Vestibular Schwannoma.
evidence.snippet: Pathogenic variants and allele-loss of the NF2 gene with Merlin loss as consequence is the driving genetic event for vestibular schwannoma development.
As many as 25% to 50% of individuals with a de novo NF2 pathogenic variant have somatic mosaicism for the variant.

nodes.description: In NF1, loss of neurofibromin removes its RAS-GTPase-activating function, so RAS-GTP accumulates and constitutively activates the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade. This is the central biochemical driver of the NF1 arm, initiating Schwann-cell neurofibroma formation and the other NF1 tissue phenotypes, and is the molecular target of MEK1/2 inhibitors such as selumetinib.

biological_processes: regulation of Ras protein signal transduction

evidence.reference_title: A RASopathy gene commonly mutated in cancer: the neurofibromatosis type 1 tumour suppressor.
evidence.snippet: The NF1 gene encodes a RAS GTPase-activating protein called neurofibromin and is one of several genes that (when mutant) affect RAS-MAPK signalling, causing related diseases collectively known as RASopathies.

nodes.description: All three arms converge on neoplastic proliferation of the Schwann-cell lineage within peripheral, spinal and cranial nerves, producing the benign nerve-sheath tumors (neurofibromas in NF1; schwannomas in NF2-related disease and schwannomatosis) that define the neurofibromatosis spectrum, together with associated CNS tumors (meningiomas, ependymomas, optic pathway gliomas).

evidence.reference_title: Cellular mechanisms of heterogeneity in NF2-mutant schwannoma.
evidence.snippet: Virtually all schwannomas result from inactivation of the NF2 tumor suppressor gene with few, if any, cooperating mutations.

nodes.description: Diffuse neurofibromas involving multiple nerve fascicles, often congenital, with a lifetime risk of malignant transformation to MPNST; the target of the MEK1/2 inhibitor selumetinib.

evidence.snippet: About half of people with NF1 have plexiform neurofibromas, but most are internal and not suspected clinically.
The phase 2 trial (SPRINT) of selumetinib in pNF resulted in at least 20% reduction in the size of pNF from baseline in 71% of patients and was associated with clinically meaningful improvements.

meta.association: Germline loss-of-function variants in SMARCB1 (a SWI/SNF core subunit) cause SMARCB1-related schwannomatosis, with elevated malignancy and meningioma risk.

evidence.reference_title: Germline loss-of-function mutations in LZTR1 predispose to an inherited disorder of multiple schwannomas.
evidence.snippet: Constitutional SMARCB1 mutations at 22q11.23 have been found in ∼50% of familial and <10% of sporadic schwannomatosis cases.

nodes.description: Stereotactic radiosurgery, most commonly gamma knife, is an alternative to microsurgery for NF2-related vestibular schwannomas. Conventional radiation therapy of NF2-associated tumors is otherwise avoided, especially in childhood, because of the substantially higher malignancy risk in NF2.

evidence.snippet: stereotactic radiosurgery, most commonly with the gamma knife, may be an alternative to surgery
Radiation therapy of NF2-associated tumors, especially in childhood, when malignancy risks are likely to be substantially higher.
